paragraphs.title: Job Falls Silent Before God's Words

answers: The LORD
Eliphaz
One of Job's friends
easy.explanation: The passage begins, “Moreover the LORD answered Job, and said.”
easy.q: Who answered Job at the beginning of the passage?

answers: His hand
His garment
His book
easy.explanation: Job says, “I will lay mine hand upon my mouth.”
easy.q: What did Job place over his mouth?

answers: Continue arguing
Speak no further
Go to war
easy.explanation: Job says, “I will proceed no further.”
easy.q: What did Job decide to do after speaking?

answers: He acknowledges his lowliness
He claims to be very strong
He says that he is leaving quickly
medium.explanation: Job recognizes his smallness and unworthiness before the LORD.
medium.q: What does Job mean when he says, “Behold, I am vile”?

answers: He argues, boasts, and then leaves
He acknowledges his condition, puts his hand over his mouth, and stops speaking
He asks to rule the world and then gives orders
medium.explanation: These actions appear in order in verses 4–5.
medium.q: What is the correct order of Job's responses?

answers: Job plans to speak many more times
Job is counting his children
Job admits that he has spoken enough
medium.explanation: Job says that he will not continue speaking.
medium.q: What does “Once have I spoken; but I will not answer: yea, twice” show?

answers: It shows that he is ready to fight
It expresses silence and the end of his argument
It hides his face from the storm
challenge.explanation: The action agrees with Job's statement that he will speak no further.
challenge.q: Why is placing his hand over his mouth an appropriate response for Job?

answers: He moves from arguing to recognizing his limitations and becoming silent
He moves from silence to ruling the world
He moves from fear to threatening the wicked
challenge.explanation: Job changes from speaking and contending to humility and silence.
challenge.q: What change takes place in Job in this passage?

answers: Job requests another answer
Job claims to have many more arguments
Job admits that he has no further answer and will stop speaking
challenge.explanation: Both statements express the stopping of Job's response before God.
challenge.q: How are “what shall I answer thee?” and “I will proceed no further” related?

paragraphs.title: The Challenge to Govern the World and Subdue the Wicked

answers: From the mountain
Out of the whirlwind
From the river
easy.explanation: The text says that the LORD answered Job “out of the whirlwind.”
easy.q: From where did the LORD answer Job?

answers: Gird up his loins like a man
Lie down in the shade
Fish for leviathan
easy.explanation: The LORD says, “Gird up thy loins now like a man.”
easy.q: What did the LORD command Job to do?

answers: The beasts of the field
The proud and the wicked
The rivers
easy.explanation: Job is told to look upon the proud and bring down the wicked.
easy.q: Whom was Job challenged to abase and tread down?

answers: Clothe or adorn yourself with greatness
Run away
Lie down to rest
medium.explanation: The LORD challenges Job to display majesty, glory, and excellence.
medium.q: What does “Deck thyself now with majesty and excellency” mean in context?

answers: Subdue the proud and wicked
Eat the produce of the mountains
Bind leviathan
medium.explanation: Job must demonstrate power and judgment by bringing down the proud and wicked.
medium.q: What must Job do before he could claim that his own right hand could save him?

answers: Whether Job would overturn God's judgment in order to justify himself
Whether Job should become a servant
Whether Job could find Behemoth
medium.explanation: The LORD asks whether Job would reject divine judgment so that he might appear righteous.
medium.q: What issue is raised by the question, “Wilt thou also disannul my judgment?”

answers: Power and the ability to subdue the wicked
The ability to rest in the shade
The ability to fish in a river
challenge.explanation: The LORD says that Job's own right hand could save him only if he could perform these mighty acts.
challenge.q: What would Job need to demonstrate in order to save himself by his own right hand?

answers: Rest, eat, and drink
Prepare himself, display power and judgment, and humble the proud
Fish, bind, and play
challenge.explanation: The sequence follows the commands and questions in verses 7–14.
challenge.q: Which sequence best describes the challenge given to Job?

answers: Job would need broad authority over the proud and wicked
Job should hide from the wicked
Job should feed the beasts of the field
challenge.explanation: The command calls for comprehensive power to judge and humble the proud.
challenge.q: What is implied by the command to look upon every proud person and abase him?

paragraphs.title: Behemoth: Strength and Peace in Nature

answers: Leviathan
Behemoth
A bird
easy.explanation: The passage begins, “Behold now behemoth, which I made with thee.”
easy.q: Which creature does the LORD present to Job?

answers: Grass as an ox
Fish
Meat
easy.explanation: The text says, “he eateth grass as an ox.”

answers: On the mountain peak
Under shady trees, among reeds and fens
Inside a city
easy.explanation: He lies under the shady trees, in the covert of the reed and fens.

answers: His bones are extremely strong and hard
His bones are weak and brittle
His bones are made of wood
medium.explanation: The comparison emphasizes the creature's great physical strength.
medium.q: What do Behemoth's bones being “as strong pieces of brass” suggest?

answers: As a small and swift creature
As a creature with powerful loins and strong bones
As a creature unable to move
medium.explanation: The passage highlights his strength in his loins and the firmness of his bones.
medium.q: How does the passage describe Behemoth's power?

answers: He lives peacefully and securely in nature
He is afraid of all water
He leaves nature and moves to the city
medium.explanation: Behemoth rests calmly and trusts that he can face the Jordan.
medium.q: What can be learned from Behemoth's resting in the shade and not hurrying when the river rises?

answers: Great strength together with peaceful life in nature
Weakness together with constant fear
Quickness together with life in a city
challenge.explanation: The passage combines descriptions of enormous strength with rest and security.
challenge.q: Which combination of qualities is most prominent in the description of Behemoth?

answers: He remains unafraid even when the Jordan reaches his mouth
He drinks only tiny amounts of water
He hides inside the river
challenge.explanation: The text says that he drinks up a river and hastens not.
challenge.q: Why does the mention of the river strengthen the description of Behemoth's security?

answers: Behemoth is presented as part of nature rather than isolated from it
Behemoth hunts every other animal
The animals are afraid to approach him
challenge.explanation: The mountains bring him food where all the beasts of the field play.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the fact that the beasts of the field play where Behemoth is?

paragraphs.title: Leviathan: The Creature That Cannot Be Captured

answers: Behemoth
Leviathan
An ox
easy.explanation: The passage asks whether a person can draw out leviathan with a hook.
easy.q: Which creature is described in these verses?

answers: A hook
A sword
A plough
easy.explanation: The text asks, “Canst thou draw out leviathan with an hook?”
easy.q: What tool is mentioned as a way of trying to catch leviathan?

answers: A servant for ever
A king
A shepherd
easy.explanation: The LORD asks, “Wilt thou take him for a servant for ever?”
easy.q: What could a person supposedly make Leviathan become?

answers: It is a barb or hook intended to pierce Leviathan's jaw
It is a royal garment
It is a vessel for drinking water
medium.explanation: The question asks whether a person could bore Leviathan's jaw through with a thorn.
medium.q: What is the purpose of the “thorn” mentioned in the passage?

answers: Hook, cord, piercing, playing with him, and making him a servant
Net, boat, food, and sleep
Sword, shield, bow, and horse
medium.explanation: The verses mention a hook, cord, thorn, play, binding, and servitude.
medium.q: Which sequence of attempts to control Leviathan appears in the passage?

answers: Whether a human being can capture and control him
Whether he eats grass
Whether he rests in the shade
medium.explanation: The questions repeatedly test the limits of human power over Leviathan.
medium.q: What do the many questions about Leviathan examine?

answers: Leviathan cannot be controlled by ordinary human means
Leviathan needs human assistance
Leviathan is smaller than a human being
challenge.explanation: The escalating examples emphasize that Leviathan cannot be captured or enslaved.
challenge.q: What is the main point of moving from a hook and cord to making Leviathan a servant?

answers: Provoking Leviathan can bring danger and painful consequences
A person must continue fighting him
Leviathan always runs away from battle
challenge.explanation: The warning tells the person to remember the outcome of the struggle and not continue.
challenge.q: What warning is conveyed by “Remember the battle, do no more”?

answers: Both demonstrate power that humans cannot easily control
Both are described as domestic animals
Both eat only fish
challenge.explanation: Behemoth is powerful and secure in nature, while Leviathan cannot be captured or enslaved.
challenge.q: What connection exists between the descriptions of Behemoth and Leviathan?
